analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from using non-compete agreements against lower-paid hourly workers.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to void non-compete agreements for hourly and lower-paid workers was introduced by a single senator, heard once in committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal wage law to make every existing non-compete agreement void for workers who are not exempt from overtime and minimum wage rules, and would bar employers from writing, extending, or renewing such agreements with them. Employers could still require workers not to share trade secrets. It also creates enforcement rights and penalties under the same wage law that covers wage violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly and lower-paid workers who are covered by federal overtime and minimum wage rules and currently face non-compete agreements — workers in fields like food service, retail, staffing, and home care who can be blocked from taking a similar job nearby or leaving an employer at all.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers covered by federal wage rules

how_it_helps.text: Existing non-compete agreements with covered workers would be void and have no effect, and employers could not enforce or threaten to enforce them.
Beginning at enactment, employers could not enter into, extend, or renew any non-compete agreement with a covered worker, with the ban taking effect 180 days after enactment.
A violation would be a prohibited act under the Fair Labor Standards Act, letting workers seek legal or equitable relief from their employer, though violators would not face imprisonment.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use non-compete agreements to hold on to hourly and lower-paid workers — including franchise chains, staffing firms, and service businesses — would lose a tool for keeping workers from switching jobs, raising their hiring and training costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers that use non-competes on hourly workers

drawbacks.text: Critics of broad non-compete bans argue employers would respond by limiting investment in training, since a trained worker can walk across the street to a competitor with no penalty.
Employers would still be allowed to bind workers to confidentiality and trade-secret agreements, so the bill leaves some restrictions on workers' post-employment options in place.
The ban reaches only workers not exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act's overtime and minimum wage rules; higher-paid workers exempt from that law could still be bound by non-competes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers affected, the benefit is direct and immediate: they could leave a bad job or take a nearby better-paying one without an agreement hanging over them. The main cost falls on employers through higher turnover and hiring costs, and the honest objection is that some employers may cut back on training or shift restrictions into confidentiality clauses. The bill is deliberately narrow — it leaves executives and other exempt workers covered by state law — so it protects the workers with the least bargaining power rather than rewriting competition policy across the board.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, and the small business committee held one hearing on it, but it never got a vote in committee or on the Senate floor and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Marco Rubio introduced the bill on January 15, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point during the Congress.
On November 14, 2019, the Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee held a hearing on the bill, which was printed as S.Hrg. 116-233.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a vote in committee or on the Senate floor, and it expired at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on non-compete agreements over hourly and lower-paid workers keep a tool they would have lost, since the agreement died without a vote and with no cosponsors of either party.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers using non-competes on hourly workers

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pursued a hearing on it in the Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: Senate
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote during the remainder of the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a single Republican with zero cosponsors from either party, so neither party took a recorded position on it.

industries.note: Fast-food, retail, and other chain employers commonly use non-competes on hourly workers; the bill would void those agreements and bar new ones, making it easier for their employees to switch jobs. The employers' interest in keeping the agreements runs against the workers' interest in changing jobs freely.
Staffing businesses use non-competes and similar restrictions to control where placed workers can go next; the ban would remove that tool for covered workers.

industries.industry: Workers covered by federal wage rules
industries.note: Hourly and lower-paid workers gain mobility, bargaining power, and access to nearby job opportunities they are currently restricted from.
